value: Both statements are individually true, but the second is not the correct explanation of the first
reasoning: The zamindars held a superior hereditary right in the land and appropriated a share of the peasant's produce, so they were an exploitative intermediary class in the standard account of the Mughal agrarian system. They also repeatedly led agrarian uprisings in seventeenth-century north India with peasant backing, generally against the imperial revenue demand. Both statements are therefore true, but leading a revolt against the state does not explain, and is not inconsistent with, exploiting the peasantry in the ordinary course of revenue collection — the two facts sit alongside each other rather than one accounting for the other.
basis: Both passes agreed on the underlying HISTORY and split only on whether Statement I is false: A read both as true with II not explaining I, B read I as false BECAUSE the zamindars led peasant-backed risings. Adjudicated to A. B's inference is a non-sequitur — leading a rising against the imperial revenue demand is fully compatible with appropriating a share of the peasant's surplus, and the two are the joint thesis of the standard treatment of the Mughal agrarian system rather than alternatives. Two further considerations point the same way: the option set itself contains 'both true but II is not the explanation', which exists precisely for a pair whose facts are independently attested but causally unrelated, and taking Statement I as false would make the exploitative character of the zamindari class a minority position rather than the textbook one. Note the confidence also favours A here (MED against B's LOW), though that was not the deciding factor — the argument was. No official key exists for this paper.
